content: Spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD) involves a separation of the layers of the coronary artery wall, which can occur within or between the intima, media, or adventitia. Two primary mechanisms have been proposed to explain this arterial wall separation. The first is the intimal tear hypothesis, where a disruption at the intimal-luminal interface allows blood to enter and accumulate in a false lumen, forming an intramural hematoma (IMH) that separates the arterial wall. The second mechanism is the medial hemorrhage hypothesis, which suggests that bleeding within the arterial wall, potentially due to spontaneous rupture of the vasa vasorum, initiates the process. While the angiographic appearance of multiple lumens is pathognomonic for SCAD, the presence of intimal disruption does not necessarily indicate the specific mechanism responsible for the tear. SCAD is increasingly recognized as a significant cause of myocardial infarction (MI), particularly in young women. Although it has been acknowledged as a distinct clinical entity since the 1930s, its pathogenesis remains poorly understood. Various hypotheses have been proposed based on clinical and pathological observations. Historically, SCAD has been underdiagnosed using angiography alone. However, advancements in intravascular imaging, particularly optical coherence tomography (OCT), have significantly improved our understanding of SCAD. OCT has revealed distinct pathological features, such as dissection flaps and intramural hematomas, and has shown promise in optimizing percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) outcomes in SCAD cases. Collaborative efforts to utilize OCT as an in vivo microscope may further elucidate this poorly understood condition. The pathophysiology of non-atherosclerotic SCAD (NA-SCAD) is not fully understood, but two mechanisms—intimal tear and vasa vasorum bleeding with intramedial hemorrhage—are thought to play a role. Both mechanisms result in the formation of a false lumen filled with intramural hematoma. Atherosclerotic SCAD, in contrast, is limited in extent due to medial atrophy and scarring, whereas NA-SCAD can involve extensive dissection lengths, particularly in the presence of arterial fragility caused by predisposing arteriopathies. Intracoronary imaging studies in NA-SCAD cases consistently show the absence of atherosclerosis. Histologically, intramural hematomas in SCAD often involve the outer two-thirds of the media. An inflammatory response, characterized by eosinophilic infiltrates in the adventitia, has been observed, suggesting periarteritis that weakens the medial-adventitial layer and predisposes the artery to dissection. However, this inflammatory response is more likely reactive rather than causative. Coronary artery tortuosity has been proposed as a potential marker or mechanism for SCAD. In a retrospective study comparing 246 SCAD patients with 313 controls, coronary tortuosity—defined as the presence of three or more consecutive curvatures of 90 to 180 degrees in a major epicardial coronary artery—was observed in 78% of SCAD patients compared to 17% of controls. However, coronary tortuosity was also associated with extracoronary vasculopathies, such as fibromuscular dysplasia, suggesting that tortuosity, like dissection, may be a manifestation of an underlying vasculopathy rather than a direct cause of SCAD. In pregnancy and the early postpartum period, SCAD may occur due to increased hemodynamic stress and hormonal effects that render the coronary arterial wall more fragile. Multiparity further increases the risk of SCAD, and dissections in other arterial beds are also more common during pregnancy. Intramural hematomas in SCAD are typically located in the outer two-thirds of the media. An eosinophilic inflammatory reaction in the adventitial layer has been described, which may contribute to arterial fragility, although it is more likely a consequence rather than a cause of the dissection.
